prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which many neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength are interrogated together, bringing optical timekeeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep B037 alone as my final position, and the round-1 exchange has strengthened it. What persuades me is the physics, not the support count. The magic-wavelength condition cancels the lattice light shift on the clock transition, so thousands of atoms can be held for long interrogation times without perturbing the frequency they are meant to report. That is a new regime relative to single trapped ions, where the figure of merit is limited by one quantum absorber, and to the comb, which is a ruler and not a clock. The regime was then shown to be robust: independent lattice clocks (Tokyo, Boulder, Paris, Braunschweig and others, in several species) agree near 1e-18 and have been intercompared over fibre links, and the same systems now show many-body effects such as spin-squeezed operation and millimetre-scale gravitational redshift. As a theorist in a neighbouring field I am looking for the combination of a clean idea, a clear experimental demonstration and reproduction across laboratories, and this entry has all three. On the chair's question about priority, my understanding, which I recall from the literature and have not re-checked against primary papers, is that Katori's group proposed the magic-wavelength lattice and demonstrated the first strontium lattice clock, and Ye's group then carried the strontium lattice clock to the accuracy and coherence frontier and connected it to the comb and to the many-body regime. Two names map onto those two separable steps. I therefore think two names are sufficient, provided the citation is tied to the magic-wavelength lattice and the record says openly that Paris, NIST and ion-clock groups also contributed. I would support a request for an expert report to verify the priority dates before the ballot.
statement.case_against: The real risk is still overlap and framing. The 1997 laser-cooling prize, the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize for control of individual quantum systems sit right next to this one, and a sceptical colleague can call the lattice clock a spectacular refinement rather than a discovery about nature. No new physics has yet been seen with these clocks, and the redefinition of the second, geodesy and constant-variation tests are partly prospective. Two names also compress a large community. I considered these points and still rate them as real but not decisive, because the magic-wavelength lattice is a distinct invention with a distinct failure mode removed and the performance gain is measured, not promised. If the priority check were to show that the first demonstration and the accuracy frontier cannot be separated cleanly between Katori and Ye, I would want to revisit the credit.

responses.point: Kroll holds that the lattice clock is an instrument-level advance with demonstrated figures of merit, notes that no new physics has yet been seen with the clocks, and asks whether a third name such as a clock-comparison or atomic-theory contributor is needed.
responses.response: I agree that the claim to defend is a demonstrated capability, not a discovery of new physics, and I think the citation should say so plainly. On a third name I would resist. The shortlist supports only Katori and Ye for this ballot, and adding a clock-comparison or theory figure would weaken the one feature that makes this entry easier to defend than the others, namely a clean two-step division between proposal and first demonstration on one side and accuracy and coherence on the other. The wider community is better acknowledged in the text than in the credit. Where I can add something as a quantum-optics theorist is on the many-body side: spin-squeezed and correlated operation in the lattice shows that the ensemble is a controllable quantum system and not only a bag of independent atoms, which supports reading it as a new regime and not as a tidier ion clock.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B037 first and wants the credit confined to the magic-wavelength lattice and not widened to optical clocks in general, while admitting that she recalls the priority history from memory.
responses.response: I agree with keeping the citation narrow, and I share your caveat about memory, since my own account of the priority order is also recalled and not checked. You are the closest of us to precision atomic theory, so I would ask you to check two points: that the magic-wavelength idea and the first lattice-clock demonstration are what I think they are, and that the contemporaneous Paris work was not decisive in a way that changes the names. The conflict question you raised for yourself cuts the other way from mine here. Your familiarity with the atomic community is the reason your reading of the priority record carries weight, and I would not treat it as a reason to discount your view. If your check supports two names I will be comfortable; if it does not, I would want to hear the alternative before the vote.

responses.point: Pearce supports B037 for the invention and demonstrated accuracy, wants the citation not to lean on the redefinition of the second, and says that as an astroparticle physicist he cannot settle the relative-merit question against ion clocks.
responses.response: I accept the wording point, and my revised citation drops any reference to the redefinition of the second, since the committee should reward what has been measured. On the ion-clock question you cannot settle, I can offer my view as someone adjacent to the field. The best ion clocks (Al+ in particular) reach comparable systematic uncertainty, but they reach it by a different route: one absorber and long averaging, against many atoms interrogated at once. That difference is exactly why the 2012 prize does not subsume the lattice clock, and why I do not think ion-clock originators are unfairly omitted by a lattice-clock citation. I would still ask that the supporting text name the ion-clock community as a parallel achievement so that the record is not misleading.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B042 but says that if the committee cannot accept the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and 3D omissions, B037 with its clean two-person attribution is the better choice and he would not stand in the way.
responses.response: Thank you, that is the most useful statement for me on the B042 side. My view of B042 has not changed on the merits: I regard Z2 topological insulators as distinct from the 2016 lineage, and I accept your and Eriksson's reading of that overlap. What keeps me from putting it first is the credit, because the HgTe experiment followed the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal and a citation to Kane, Mele and Molenkamp cannot fully repair that. If the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang question can be handled in the citation to your satisfaction, B042 is a prize I could vote for, and I keep it as my first alternative. I would simply say that the two options are not symmetric: the B037 credit needs a priority check that I expect to hold, while the B042 credit has a known gap that no check can close.

responses.point: Olsson prefers B042 because it credits Mele and gives the most defensible mapping of who did what first, regrets losing Xue's quantum anomalous Hall experiment, and says she would hear the physics on B008 from me while weighing my ranking separately.
responses.response: I appreciate that, and I will be direct about circuit QED: the physics is strong and the experiments are real, but I will not argue for B008 and I will recuse myself from any decision on it. On B042, I agree that dropping Mele would leave an arbitrary gap on the theory side, and I would not support B012 over B042 for that reason. I do not see how Xue's anomalous Hall experiment can be accommodated without a second part, and I would not stack it, since that would put two prizes on one field and break the three-person limit. My difference from you is in what I weight most heavily. For me the decisive factor is a credit that survives a priority check, and on that B037 looks more secure, though I would defend B042 as a legitimate prize if the committee chose it.

responses.point: Eriksson moved from B018 to B042, argues that the Z2 insulators are a distinct, later discovery than the 2016 topological prize, and agrees that a second superconducting-circuit prize is hard to justify.
responses.response: I have no objection to your reading of the 2016 prize. Thouless, Haldane and Kosterlitz are about topological phase transitions and Chern-type invariants in the quantum Hall and Haldane setting, and a time-reversal-invariant Z2 insulator is a different thing, with materials realisations in HgTe, InAs/GaSb and Bi-based compounds. We differ on the final ordering and I think narrowly. The decisive test for me is whether the credit can be written without leaving out someone whose contribution was the enabling step, and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal is exactly that for HgTe. That is why B042 stays second for me. I also take your advice on B008 and I will leave it as a recused alternative and not a part of my configuration.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as a distinct new regime and not as a refinement of the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.

Whether my recalled priority history of Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and first strontium lattice clock, and Ye's later accuracy and many-body work, survives a primary-source or expert check; I have not verified it.
Whether two names are sufficient given the Paris, NIST and ion-clock contributions, and how openly the supporting text should acknowledge them.
How much the still-pending redefinition of the second should count, which I would prefer to treat as context and not as part of the citation.
Whether B042 can be given a credit that honours the Z2 prediction and the HgTe observation without implying the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and 3D contributions.
statement.conflict_note: I am director of the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology at Chalmers and work closely with the superconducting-circuit community, so B008 (Blais, Wallraff, Schoelkopf) is my own field. I ranked it first in the opening round, I have removed it from my preferred configuration, and I would recuse myself from any decision on it; I list it only as a second alternative and ask that the committee treat that listing with caution. I have no personal or institutional tie to Katori, Ye, Kane, Mele or Molenkamp. Chalmers colleagues in the Gothenburg physics environment (Mehlig, Olsson) are noted, with no collaboration with the credited names.
